title: Cholinergic Drugs — Mechanism and Key Use
description: Flip each card to reveal the mechanism and primary clinical use.

dialogs.answer: Direct-acting muscarinic agonist. Used in glaucoma (contracts ciliary muscle → opens trabecular meshwork → ↓IOP) and Sjögren's syndrome (stimulates salivary secretion).

tips.front: Think: which direct M agonist is used in the eye?

dialogs.answer: Direct-acting M3 agonist resistant to AChE hydrolysis. Used in post-operative urinary retention and paralytic ileus (increases detrusor and GI smooth muscle tone).

tips.front: Think: which M agonist restores bladder and gut motility?

dialogs.answer: Reversible AChE inhibitor — quaternary amine (does NOT cross BBB). Used to reverse non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade and in myasthenia gravis.

tips.front: Think: quaternary = no BBB crossing. Used at the NMJ.

dialogs.answer: Reversible AChE inhibitor — tertiary amine (CROSSES BBB). Antidote for anticholinergic toxicity (atropine overdose) because of its CNS penetration.

tips.front: Think: tertiary = crosses BBB. The antidote that reaches the brain.

dialogs.answer: Reversible AChE inhibitor — tertiary amine (crosses BBB). Used in Alzheimer's disease to boost central cholinergic transmission. Once-daily dosing, well tolerated.

tips.front: Think: which AChE inhibitor is used for dementia?
